prompt: An appraiser values a 10-year-old office building in Ocala. The site is worth $150,000, replacement cost new is $900,000, and the building has a 50-year economic life with straight-line depreciation. What value does the cost approach indicate?
explanation: Cost approach = replacement cost new − accrued depreciation + site value. Depreciation is 10/50 = 20% of $900,000 = $180,000, leaving a depreciated building of $720,000. Adding the $150,000 site gives $870,000. Land does not wear out, so it is added after depreciation, not depreciated.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at the depreciated building value ($720,000) and forgets to add the $150,000 site value back in.
distractorExplanations.b: Depreciates the land along with the building (80% of $1,050,000); land is not depreciated in the cost approach.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds site value to replacement cost new but skips the $180,000 of accrued depreciation on a 10-year-old building.

prompt: Sarasota zoning allows backyard accessory dwellings, but a subdivision's recorded deed restrictions limit each lot to one single-family residence. A buyer plans to add a rental cottage after closing. Which rule controls what she can build?

options.text: Zoning, because public law overrides private covenants
Zoning, once the county issues a building permit
The deed restriction, as the stricter rule
Whichever rule was adopted most recently

explanation: Zoning and recorded deed restrictions both bind the lot, and the owner must satisfy each one. When they conflict, the more restrictive rule effectively controls: zoning permission does not cancel a private covenant, which other lot owners or the association can enforce by injunction. The buyer should read the restrictions before relying on zoning.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses permission with override: zoning sets a public floor but does not erase stricter private covenants recorded on the lot.
distractorExplanations.b: A permit shows zoning compliance only; it does not release a recorded covenant, so neighbors or the HOA can still sue to enforce it.
distractorExplanations.d: Recency is not the test; both sets of rules bind the owner at once, and the more restrictive one sets the practical limit.
